newsitem.title: ROMANIA: Romanians demand truth about 1989 revolution.
newsitem.headline: Romanians demand truth about 1989 revolution.

text.p: BUCHAREST, Dec 21, Reuter - Romanians on Saturday marked the seventh anniversary of the revolt that ended communist rule, with many calling on the newly-elected authorities to explain why more than 1,000 people were killed.

Hundreds of people, many mourning dead relatives, braved icy rain in a Bucharest cemetery to lay wreaths, light candles and pray for those killed during the revolt which rocked the capital on December 21-22, 1989.

"Mister President, please find out the truth and punish the criminals," blurted out a man in the crowd at the Heroes' Cemetery as President Emil Constantinescu laid a wreath in a silent ceremony less than a month after taking office.
More than 500 people were shot dead in Bucharest by forces loyal to dictator Nicolae Ceausescu and over 1,000 were killed throughout the country of 23 million.

A religious service was planned later in the day in University Square, where dozens were shot or crushed by armoured vehicles during the upheaval. Similar ceremonies were planned in several major cities.
The silent ceremonies replaced the protests over the past six years when thousands marched through the capital shouting slogans against then-president Ion Iliescu.
Iliescu, a communist who took power during the 1989 revolt, remained in office until being ousted in last month's election.

"Before my son went out to fight he said 'Mom, don't worry. I'll come home after we win.' But he never returned," Rozalia Stefanov, tears streaming down her face, said while caressing a photograph of her son Victor, 18 at the time of the revolt.
"Those who masterminded the revolt needed victims to make the new authorities credible," said Ion Iofciu, a leader of the December 21 Association.
Near Stefanov's grave, a white marble cross atop another grave honoured Andrei Burcioaica, who died aged 13.
Burcioaica was run over by an armoured carrier trying to disperse protesters outside Ceausescu's office.

Many liberals share Iofciu's view that the explosion of anger by young people fighting heavily armed security forces with their bare hands was hijacked by reformist communists, including Iliescu, to remain in power.

Only about 300 of the victims died before Ceausescu climbed aboard a helicopter on the roof of the Communist Party Central Committee headquarters on December 22 and fled Bucharest. He and his wife Elena were caught, summarily tried and executed on Christmas Day.
Official reports have since suggested that most of the victims were shot by mysterious snipers dubbed "terrorists". Not a single "terrorist" has yet been brought to trial.

A parliamentary session devoted to the anniversary on Friday degenerated into a row over what had actually occurred during the December 1989 events. Constantinescu told the sitting that authorities had a year to determine the truth.
"We will continue our investigations into the 1989 events," Virgil Magureanu head of the country's intelligence service, told Reuters at the graveside service.
"It is our duty to find out the truth," said Magureanu, one of the panel of accusers who passed the death sentence on Ceausescu.
